author: original (NevaIB)
title: From models to materials
bigPicture: Real materials rarely fit one bonding type perfectly. The bonding triangle places a substance between ionic, covalent and metallic using electronegativity, and that position predicts its properties. Alloys and polymers show how chemists design materials from these bonding ideas.

keyIdeas.answer: Ionic, covalent and metallic are idealised models; most substances have a mixture of character. The triangular bonding diagram (data booklet) shows this continuum and lets you explain a material's properties.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you place a binary compound on the bonding triangle?
keyIdeas.answer: x-axis: average electronegativity of the two elements; y-axis: difference in electronegativity. Large difference → ionic (top); small difference with high average → covalent (bottom right); small difference with low average → metallic (bottom left). E.g. NaCl (Δχ 2.3, average 2.05) is ionic; SiCl₄ polar covalent. Predict properties from position. No % ionic character calculations.

keyIdeas.cue: What are alloys and why are they useful?
keyIdeas.answer: Mixtures of a metal with other metals or non-metals (bronze, brass, steel). Different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, so layers slide less: harder and stronger; can also resist corrosion (stainless steel). Metallic bonding is non-directional, so different atoms can be mixed in.

keyIdeas.cue: How does structure explain the properties of plastics?
keyIdeas.answer: Polymers are macromolecules of many repeating units (monomers). Long chains tangle and have many London forces → flexible, low density, often strong; usually electrical insulators; most are not biodegradable. Natural polymers include starch, cellulose, proteins and DNA; synthetic include polythene and PVC.

The C=C of each alkene monomer opens and monomers join into a chain; nothing else is produced. Draw the repeating unit by taking the two C=C carbons as a single-bonded unit with continuation bonds through brackets, e.g. poly(chloroethene): –[CH₂–CHCl]ₙ–. Monomers are given or deduced from the polymer.

Monomers with two functional groups join with loss of a small molecule (usually H₂O). Polyesters: diol + dicarboxylic acid → ester links –COO–. Polyamides: diamine + dicarboxylic acid → amide links –CONH–. Biological macromolecules (proteins, polysaccharides, nucleic acids) form by condensation and break down by hydrolysis.

keyTerms.def: Diagram of average electronegativity against electronegativity difference, with ionic, covalent and metallic corners.
Mixture of a metal with other elements, with enhanced properties.
Small molecule that joins to form a polymer.
Section of a polymer that repeats; drawn in brackets with continuation bonds.
Formed by opening C=C bonds; no other product.
Formed with loss of a small molecule such as water (AHL).

workedExamples.title: Using the triangle
workedExamples.prompt: Electronegativities: Al 1.6, Cl 3.2, O 3.4. Locate AlCl₃ and Al₂O₃.
steps: AlCl₃: average 2.4, difference 1.6 → polar covalent region.
Al₂O₃: average 2.5, difference 1.8 → border of polar covalent and ionic.
workedExamples.answer: AlCl₃ mainly polar covalent (sublimes at low temperature); Al₂O₃ more ionic (very high melting point).

workedExamples.title: Repeating unit
workedExamples.prompt: Draw the repeating unit of poly(propene) from propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃.
steps: Put in brackets with continuation bonds.

misconceptions.wrong: The CH₃ in propene ends up in the main chain.
misconceptions.right: Only the two C=C carbons form the backbone; CH₃ is a side group.
They are mixtures; composition can vary.
Proteins, starch, cellulose and DNA are natural polymers.

paper1B.data: Electronegativity data: Mg 1.3, Si 1.9, S 2.6, O 3.4.
paper1B.prompt: Use the bonding triangle to compare the bonding in MgO and SiO₂ and link to one property of each.
paper1B.answer: MgO: Δχ 2.1, average 2.35 → ionic; conducts when molten. SiO₂: Δχ 1.5, average 2.65 → polar covalent (giant covalent network); very high melting point, doesn't conduct.
